chapters.title: Book VI: The Widow And The Wife — Chapter LV
paragraphs:
Does she have faults? I wish you shared them.
They are the ferment of the finest wine;
Or call them fire that makes a substance new,
The fire that changes dense, black matter
Into a crystal road for sunlight.

If youth is a time of hope, that often means only that older people have hopes for us. No one is more likely than the young to believe that their feelings, their farewells, and their resolutions can never be repeated. Every crisis feels final simply because it is new. We are told that even the oldest people in Peru are still disturbed by earthquakes; but they probably look beyond each shock and remember that there will be plenty more.

Dorothea was still at that age when eyes framed by long, thick lashes can emerge from a shower of tears as fresh and untired as a newly opened passion-flower. To her, that morning's farewell to Will Ladislaw seemed to end their personal connection. He was disappearing into an unknown stretch of years, and if he ever returned, he would be a different man. She had no idea of his actual thoughts: his proud determination to disprove in advance any suspicion that he was a penniless adventurer pursuing a rich woman. She had readily explained everything he did by assuming that Mr. Casaubon's codicil seemed to him, as it did to her, a brutal, cruel ban on any continuing friendship between them. Their youthful pleasure in talking together, in saying things no one else would have cared to hear, was over forever, a treasure belonging to the past. Precisely for that reason, she let herself dwell on it without restraint. That unique happiness was dead too, and in its dark, silent room she could release a passionate grief that astonished even her. For the first time, she took the miniature off the wall and kept it in front of her. She liked to bring together in her thoughts the woman who had been judged too harshly and the grandson whom both her heart and her reason defended. Could anyone who has delighted in a woman's tenderness blame her for cupping the small oval picture in her hand, making a bed for it there, and resting her cheek against it, as though this could comfort those unjustly condemned? She did not yet understand that Love had briefly visited her, like a dream just before waking, his wings bright with the colors of dawn. She did not know it was to Love that she was sobbing her farewell, as his image vanished before the blameless severity of inescapable daylight. She felt only that something in her life was irreparably wrong, something lost; and this made her thoughts about the future turn all the more readily into resolutions. Passionate people, eager to build their future lives, are apt to pledge themselves to making their own visions real.

One day Dorothea went to Freshitt, as she had promised, to stay overnight and watch the baby being washed. Mrs. Cadwallader came to dinner; the Rector was away fishing. The evening was warm. Even in the lovely drawing room, whose open window looked down over fine old turf to a lily pond and carefully planted mounds, the heat was enough to make Celia, in her white muslin and loose curls, pity Dodo in her black dress and close-fitting cap. She did not think of this, however, until various proceedings involving the baby were over and her mind was free again. She had been sitting with a fan for some time before she said, in her quiet, throaty voice,
“Dear Dodo, please take that cap off. Your clothes must be making you feel quite ill.”
“I've grown so used to it—it's become a kind of shell,” Dorothea said with a smile. “Without it I feel rather naked and exposed.”

“I insist on seeing you without it. Just looking at it makes us all hot,” said Celia. She put down her fan and went over to Dorothea. The little woman in white muslin made a pretty picture as she undid the widow's cap on her more majestic sister's head and tossed it onto a chair. Sir James entered just as the coils and braids of dark brown hair were freed. He looked at the uncovered head and gave a satisfied “Ah!”
“That was my doing, James,” Celia said. “Dodo needn't be such a slave to mourning. She needn't wear that cap with her friends anymore.”
“My dear Celia,” Lady Chettam said, “a widow has to stay in mourning for at least a year.”
“Unless she marries again before the year's up,” said Mrs. Cadwallader, who rather enjoyed shocking her good friend the Dowager. Annoyed, Sir James bent forward to play with Celia's Maltese dog.

“I hope that very seldom happens,” said Lady Chettam, in a voice intended to prevent it. “None of our friends ever did such a thing except Mrs. Beevor, and Lord Grinsell was deeply distressed by it. Her first husband was objectionable, which made it all the more extraordinary. And she paid dearly for it. They said Captain Beevor pulled her about by her hair and pointed loaded pistols at her.”

“Well, if she chose the wrong man!” said Mrs. Cadwallader, now feeling thoroughly mischievous. “Then marriage is always a bad business, whether it's the first or the second. Having come first isn't much of a recommendation in a husband who has nothing else to recommend him. I'd sooner have a good second husband than a mediocre first.”
“My dear, you let that clever tongue of yours run away with you,” said Lady Chettam. “I'm sure you would be the very last woman to remarry too soon if our dear Rector were taken from us.”

“Oh, I won't make promises. It might be necessary to save money. Remarrying is permitted, I suppose; otherwise we might as well be Hindus as Christians. Naturally, if a woman accepts the wrong man, she must live with the consequences, and if she does it twice she deserves what she gets. But if she can marry good birth, good looks, and courage, the sooner she does it the better.”
“I consider this a very unfortunate choice of conversation,” said Sir James, looking disgusted. “Let's talk about something else.”

“Please don't change it for my sake, Sir James,” said Dorothea. She was determined to use this opportunity to put an end to the hints about excellent prospective husbands. “If you're speaking on my behalf, I assure you that nothing could be more impersonal or less interesting to me than a second marriage. It concerns me no more than a discussion of women going fox-hunting. Whether I admire them for it or not, I won't be joining them. Please let Mrs. Cadwallader entertain herself with this subject as freely as with any other.”

“My dear Mrs. Casaubon,” said Lady Chettam with her utmost dignity, “I hope you don't imagine I was referring to you when I mentioned Mrs. Beevor. Hers was simply a case that came to mind. She was Lord Grinsell's stepdaughter: his second wife was Mrs. Teveroy. There could not possibly have been any reference to you.”
“Of course not,” Celia said. “Nobody chose the subject. It all started with Dodo's cap. What Mrs. Cadwallader said was perfectly true. A woman couldn't get married wearing a widow's cap, James.”

“Quiet, my dear!” said Mrs. Cadwallader. “I won't misbehave again. I won't so much as mention Dido or Zenobia. But what shall we talk about? Personally, I object to discussing Human Nature, since that is the nature rectors' wives happen to have.”

Later that evening, when Mrs. Cadwallader had left, Celia said to Dorothea in private, “Really, Dodo, removing that cap made you yourself again in more than one way. You spoke up exactly as you used to when someone said something you didn't like. Only I couldn't quite tell whether you thought James was wrong or Mrs. Cadwallader.”

“Neither of them,” said Dorothea. “James was being considerate of me, but he was wrong to think Mrs. Cadwallader's remarks upset me. They would only upset me if there were a law forcing me to accept any specimen of good birth and good looks that she or anyone else recommended.”

“Still, Dodo, if you ever did get married, good birth and good looks would make it all the better,” Celia said. She was thinking that Mr. Casaubon had been poorly supplied with those advantages, and that Dorothea ought to be warned in time.

“Don't worry, Kitty. I have quite different ideas for my life. I'm never going to marry again,” Dorothea said, touching her sister's chin and looking at her with affectionate indulgence. Celia was feeding her baby, and Dorothea had come to wish her good night.
“Really? Absolutely?” said Celia. “No one at all—even if he were quite extraordinary?”

Dorothea slowly shook her head. “No one at all. I have such lovely plans. I'd like to take a large piece of land, drain it, and establish a little community where everyone worked and all the work was properly done. I would know every person there and be their friend. I'm going to consult Mr. Garth at length. He can tell me almost everything I need to know.”
“So you _will_ be happy as long as you have a plan, Dodo?” Celia asked. “Perhaps little Arthur will like making plans when he's older, and then he can help you.”

That very night Sir James learned that Dorothea was quite determined never to marry anyone and was going to occupy herself with “all sorts of plans,” just as she used to. He said nothing. Privately, he found something repellent in a woman's marrying for a second time; no possible husband could keep him from feeling that for Dorothea it would be a kind of desecration. He knew the world would find that feeling absurd, especially about a woman of twenty-one. The world's habit was to discuss a young widow's remarriage as inevitable and probably imminent, and to smile knowingly when she behaved accordingly. But if Dorothea chose to bind herself to solitude, he felt that such a decision would suit her well.

chapters.title: Book VI: The Widow And The Wife — Chapter LVI
paragraphs:
“How fortunate the man, by birth and learning,
Who does not serve another person's will;
Whose honest thoughts provide his armor,
Whose only art is simple truth!
. . . . . . .
This man escapes the bonds of servitude:
The hope of rising and the fear of falling.
He owns himself, though he may own no land;
Possessing nothing, he possesses all.”
—SIR HENRY WOTTON.

Dorothea's trust in Caleb Garth's knowledge had begun when she heard that he approved of her cottages. It grew rapidly during her stay at Freshitt. Sir James persuaded her to ride over both estates with him and Caleb, who fully shared her admiration. He told his wife that Mrs. Casaubon had an understanding of business most unusual in a woman. Remember that by “business” Caleb never meant dealings in money, but the skillful use of labor.

“Most unusual!” Caleb repeated. “She said something I often thought myself as a boy: ‘Mr. Garth, if I live to be old, I'd like to feel that I had improved a large stretch of land and built plenty of good cottages, because the work is healthy while people are doing it, and once it's finished their lives are better for it.’ Those were her exact words. That's how deeply she understands things.”
“But she's womanly, I hope,” said Mrs. Garth. She half suspected that Mrs. Casaubon might not properly appreciate a woman's subordinate place.

“Oh, you can't imagine!” Caleb said, shaking his head. “You'd love to hear her talk, Susan. Such plain words, and a voice like music. Bless me, it reminds me of passages in the ‘Messiah’—‘and straightway there appeared a multitude of the heavenly host, praising God and saying.’ There's a quality in it that satisfies the ear.”

Caleb loved music. Whenever he could afford it, he attended any oratorio performed within reach. He came home filled with profound reverence for that mighty structure of sound, and would sit thoughtfully staring at the floor, his outstretched hands expressing a great deal that words could not.

Given their mutual understanding, it was natural that Dorothea should ask Mr. Garth to manage the business of the three farms and the many rented properties belonging to Lowick Manor. His expectation of finding enough work for two people was rapidly being fulfilled. As he put it, “Business breeds.” One kind of business beginning to breed at that time was railway construction. A proposed line would cross Lowick parish, where cattle had until then grazed in peace, without anything to astonish them. In this way the early struggles of the railway system entered Caleb Garth's affairs, and determined the course of this story for two people dear to him. Building a railway beneath the sea may have its difficulties; but the seabed is not divided among different landowners who demand compensation for injuries to their feelings as well as their property. In the district containing Middlemarch, railways caused as much excitement as the Reform Bill or the approaching terrors of cholera. Women and landowners had the firmest opinions. Women of all ages thought steam travel presumptuous and dangerous. Their argument against it was that nothing would ever persuade them to enter a railway carriage. Landowners might differ in their reasoning as widely as Mr. Solomon Featherstone differed from Lord Medlicote, but they agreed on one point: whether you sold land to the Enemy of mankind or to a company compelled to buy it, such destructive powers must pay landowners very handsomely for permission to injure the human race.

Slower minds, however, such as those of Mr. Solomon and Mrs. Waule, who both occupied their own land, took a long time to reach this conclusion. Their thoughts stuck at the vivid prospect of cutting the Big Pasture in half and leaving triangular pieces that would be “no good anyhow.” Bridges to connect the severed land, and large payments in compensation, seemed distant and unbelievable.

“Every cow will lose her calf, brother,” said Mrs. Waule in deep gloom, “if the railway crosses the Near Close. And I wouldn't be surprised if the mare did too, if she were in foal. It's a poor state of things if they can dig away a widow's property and the law has nothing to say. Once they start, what's to stop them cutting anywhere they please? Everyone knows _I_ can't fight.”

“Best say nothing, and get somebody to send them off with a flea in their ear when they come snooping and measuring,” Solomon said. “That's what people did near Brassing, as far as I understand. This talk about having to take one particular route is all a sham, if the truth were known. Let them cut through another parish. And I don't believe they'll pay anything to make up for bringing a pack of ruffians to trample your crops. Where does a company keep its pocket?”
“Brother Peter—God forgive him—got money out of a company,” said Mrs. Waule. “But that was for manganese. It wasn't for railways blowing you to pieces on every side.”

“Well, Jane, there's this,” Mr. Solomon concluded, cautiously lowering his voice. “The more obstacles we put in their way, the more they'll pay to be allowed through—if they're coming whether we like it or not.”

Mr. Solomon's reasoning was perhaps less sound than he supposed. His cunning had about as much bearing on the progress of railways as a diplomat's cunning has on a general chill or cold afflicting the solar system. Still, he acted on his views in a thoroughly diplomatic fashion: he encouraged suspicion. His side of Lowick was furthest from the village. The laborers lived either in isolated cottages or in the hamlet of Frick, where a watermill and some quarries formed a small center of slow, heavy-shouldered industry.

No one in Frick knew precisely what railways were, but public opinion opposed them. In that grassy corner, the human mind showed none of its proverbial admiration for the unknown. Instead, people assumed that unfamiliar things were likely to hurt the poor man, and that suspicion was the only sensible response. Even rumors of Reform had inspired no visions of a golden age in Frick. There was no definite promise of free grain to fatten Hiram Ford's pig, or a landlord at the “Weights and Scales” who would brew beer for nothing, or an offer from the three neighboring farmers to raise winter wages. Without any clear benefit of that sort among its promises, Reform sounded like a peddler's boasting, which warned any knowing person to be on guard. Frick's men were not badly fed. They were more disposed to a sturdy, muscular distrust than to fanaticism; less inclined to think that heaven took special care of them than that heaven itself was rather likely to cheat them—a tendency plainly visible in the weather.

Frick's outlook was therefore exactly suited to Mr. Solomon Featherstone's influence. He had a more abundant stock of the same ideas, and his suspicion of heaven and earth was better fed and had more leisure. At the time, Solomon supervised the roads. Riding his slow-paced cob, he often made his rounds through Frick to watch the men quarrying stone. He would stop with a mysterious deliberateness which might have made you imagine he had some reason to stay beyond simply lacking the impulse to move. After watching whatever work was going on for a long time, he would lift his eyes a little and study the horizon. Eventually he shook the bridle, touched the horse with his whip, and persuaded it to proceed slowly. A clock's hour hand was quick compared with Mr. Solomon, who enjoyed knowing that he could afford to take his time. He habitually stopped beside every hedger or ditcher for a cautious conversation full of vague designs. He was especially willing to hear news he had already heard, feeling that his partial disbelief gave him an advantage over any storyteller. One day, though, he himself supplied information in a conversation with Hiram Ford, a wagon driver. He asked whether Hiram had seen fellows with staffs and instruments snooping around. They called themselves railway people, but who knew what they really were or what they intended? At the very least, they claimed they were going to cut Lowick parish to pieces.
“Why, we won't be able to get from one place to another,” Hiram said, thinking of his wagon and horses.

“Not at all,” said Mr. Solomon. “And cutting up fine land like we've got in this parish! Let them go into Tipton, I say. But who knows what's behind it? Trade's the reason they give, but in the long run it's the land and the poor man that'll suffer.”
“London fellows, I reckon,” said Hiram, who had a vague idea of London as a center of hostility toward the countryside.

“Yes, certainly. And in places near Brassing, from what I've heard, people attacked them while they were spying, smashed those peeping instruments they carry, and drove them off. They knew better than to come back.”
“Must have been good fun, I'll bet,” said Hiram, whose opportunities for amusement were severely limited.

“Well, I wouldn't interfere with them myself,” Solomon said. “But some say this country's best days are over. The sign of it is these fellows overrunning it, trampling everywhere and wanting to slice it into railways. All so the big trade can swallow the little, till there's not a team of horses left on the land, nor a whip to crack.”
“I'll crack _my_ whip round their ears before they get that far,” said Hiram, as Mr. Solomon shook his bridle and moved on.

Nettle seeds need no soil preparation. The railways' destruction of the countryside became a subject of conversation not only at the “Weights and Scales,” but also in the hayfield. The gathering of workers there offered chances to talk that were rare in the rest of the farming year.

One morning, shortly after the conversation in which Mary Garth admitted her feelings for Fred Vincy to Mr. Farebrother, business took her father to Yoddrell's farm, toward Frick. He had to measure and value an outlying piece of Lowick Manor land which he expected to sell profitably for Dorothea. It must be admitted that Caleb favored getting the best possible terms out of railway companies. He left his gig at Yoddrell's and walked with his assistant and measuring chain to the land. On the way he met the company's agents, who were adjusting their spirit level. After a brief conversation, he left them, remarking that their work would soon bring them back to him at the spot he was going to measure. It was one of those gray mornings after light rain that become delightful around noon, when the clouds open a little and the earth smells sweet along lanes and hedges.

That smell would have been sweeter to Fred Vincy, riding along the lanes, had he not been troubled by fruitless attempts to decide what to do. On one side his father expected him to enter the Church at once; on the other, Mary threatened to give him up if he did. Meanwhile, the everyday working world showed no eagerness for a young gentleman with no capital and no particular skills. For someone of Fred's temperament, matters were made harder by his father's good humor. Believing his son had stopped resisting, Mr. Vincy had sent him on this pleasant ride to inquire about some greyhounds. Even once Fred decided what to do, he would still have to tell his father. But the decision, which had to come first, was admittedly the harder task. What secular occupation existed for a young man whose friends could not secure him an “appointment,” which was gentlemanly, profitable, and required no specialized knowledge? Riding near Frick in this mood, he slowed down to consider whether he dared go round by Lowick Parsonage to see Mary. He could look over the hedges from field to field. Suddenly a noise caught his attention. Across a field on his left, six or seven men in smocks, carrying hayforks, were advancing threateningly on four railway agents who faced them. Caleb Garth and his assistant were hurrying across to help the threatened party. Fred lost a few moments finding the gate. Before he could gallop up, the smocked men—who had found turning hay less urgent after their midday beer—were driving the men in coats ahead of them with their forks. Caleb's assistant, a boy of seventeen, had picked up the spirit level at Caleb's order, and had been knocked down. He seemed to be lying helpless. The men in coats could run faster, and Fred covered their retreat by riding in front of the pursuers and charging suddenly enough to disrupt the chase. “What do you think you're doing, you damned fools?” he shouted. He rode zigzag after the scattered group, slashing to either side with his whip. “I'll identify every one of you before the magistrate. You've knocked that boy down and killed him, for all I know. You'll all be hanged at the next assizes if you're not careful.” Later, Fred laughed heartily when he remembered his own words.

The laborers had been driven back through the gate into their hayfield, and Fred had reined in his horse, when Hiram Ford decided he was far enough away to issue a safe challenge. Turning back, he shouted a defiance he did not know was Homeric.
“You're a coward, that's what you are. Get off your horse, young master, and I'll fight you. You daren't come without your horse and whip. I'd soon knock the wind out of you, I would.”

“Wait a minute. I'll be back shortly, and I'll fight every one of you in turn if you like,” Fred said, confident of his boxing abilities against these dearly beloved brethren. Just now, though, he wanted to hurry back to Caleb and the fallen boy.
The boy had sprained his ankle and was in considerable pain, but had no other injury. Fred put him on the horse so that he could ride to Yoddrell's and be looked after there.
“Have them stable the horse, and tell the surveyors they can fetch their equipment,” Fred said. “It's safe now.”

“No, no,” said Caleb. “Something's broken here. They'll have to stop for today, and that's probably best. Here, Tom, take these things on the horse in front of you. When they see you coming, they'll turn back.”
“I'm glad I happened along at the right moment, Mr. Garth,” Fred said as Tom rode off. “Who knows what would have happened if the cavalry hadn't arrived in time?”

“Yes, yes, lucky indeed,” said Caleb rather absently. He was looking toward the place where he had been working when they were interrupted. “But—damn it—this is what happens when men behave like fools. My day's work is held up. I can't manage without someone to help with the measuring chain. Still!” Looking annoyed, he began walking toward the spot, apparently forgetting Fred was there. Then he suddenly turned and asked briskly, “What have you got to do today, young fellow?”
“Nothing, Mr. Garth. I'd be delighted to help. Could I?” Fred felt that helping Mary's father would itself be a way of courting her.
“Well, you mustn't object to bending down and getting hot.”
“I don't mind any of that. Only first I want a round with that hulking fellow who challenged me. It would teach him a good lesson. I won't be five minutes.”
“Don't be ridiculous!” said Caleb in his most commanding voice. “I'll speak to the men myself. It's ignorance, all of it. Someone's been feeding them lies. The poor fools don't know any better.”
“Then I'll come along,” Fred said.
“No, no, stay here. I don't need your young hot blood. I can look after myself.”

Caleb was a strong man who scarcely knew fear, except the fear of hurting other people and the fear of making speeches. Now, however, he felt obliged to deliver a small address. Having always worked hard himself, he combined strict ideas about workers with remarkable practical tolerance toward them. He believed that putting in a full day's work, and doing it well, was part of their well-being, as it was the chief source of his own happiness. But he also felt a strong fellowship with them. When he approached, the laborers had not resumed work. They stood in that rural grouping in which each man turns one shoulder toward another, two or three yards away. They looked sulkily at Caleb. He walked quickly, one hand in his pocket and the other tucked between his waistcoat buttons, and stopped among them with his usual mild expression.

“Well, my lads, what's all this?” he began. As usual he spoke in short phrases that seemed full of meaning to him because so many thoughts lay beneath them, like the spreading roots of a plant barely visible above the water. “How did you come to make such a mistake? Somebody's been lying to you. You thought those men over there meant mischief.”
“Aye,” each man answered at a different moment, according to how long it took him to find a reply.

“Nonsense! They mean nothing of the kind. They're finding out where the railway should run. Now, lads, you can't stop the railway. It'll be built whether you like it or not. Fight it and you'll get yourselves into trouble. The law allows those men onto this land. The owner can't object, and if you interfere you'll have the constable and Justice Blakesley to deal with, and handcuffs, and Middlemarch jail. You could be facing all that already, if anyone reported you.”
Caleb paused. Perhaps the finest orator could not have chosen a better moment to pause, or more effective images for this audience.

“But come now, you didn't mean harm. Someone told you the railway was a bad thing. That was a lie. It may do some harm here and there, to this person or that. So does the sun in the sky. But the railway's a good thing.”

“Aye, good for the big folk to make money from,” said old Timothy Cooper. He had stayed behind turning hay while the others went off on their adventure. “I've seen plenty come along since I was young: war and peace, the canals, old King George, the Regent, the new King George, and the new one with a different name. It's all been the same to the poor man. What have canals done for him? They've brought him neither meat nor bacon, nor wages he can save without starving himself to do it. Things have got worse for him since my young days. It'll be the same with railways. They'll only leave the poor man further behind. But anyone who interferes is a fool, and I told these fellows so. This world belongs to the big folk. And you're on their side, Mr. Garth, you are.”

Timothy was a wiry old laborer of a kind still surviving then. He kept his savings in the foot of a stocking, lived in a solitary cottage, and no amount of eloquence could sway him. He had as little feudal loyalty and as little faith as though he had actually read the Age of Reason and the Rights of Man, of which he knew absolutely nothing. Caleb faced a difficulty familiar to anyone who, in unenlightened times and without miraculous assistance, tries to reason with country people who possess an undeniable truth. They have learned it through painful experience, and can drop it like a giant's club on your delicately carved argument for a social benefit they cannot feel. Caleb had no stock of pious platitudes, even if he had wished to use them. His customary way of meeting such difficulties was simply to carry out his “business” faithfully. He answered:

“If you don't think much of me, Tim, never mind. That's not the point just now. Things may be bad for the poor man—they are bad. But I don't want these lads making things worse for themselves. Cattle may be pulling a heavy load, but tipping it into a roadside pit won't help them when some of it is their own feed.”
“We only wanted a bit of fun,” said Hiram, beginning to see the consequences. “That's all we were after.”
“Well then, promise me you won't interfere again, and I'll make sure nobody reports you.”
“I haven't interfered, and I've no need to promise,” Timothy said.
“No, but the others have. Come, I'm working as hard as any of you today, and I haven't much time to spare. Say you'll keep quiet without needing the constable.”
“Aye, we won't interfere. They can do as they please for all we care.” In such words Caleb received their promises, then hurried back to Fred, who had followed him and watched from the gateway.

They began work, and Fred helped energetically. His spirits had lifted. He even thoroughly enjoyed a good slide in the damp earth under the hedge, which dirtied his immaculate summer trousers. Was he elated by his successful charge, or pleased to help Mary's father? There was more to it. The morning's accidents had helped his stalled imagination picture a kind of employment that offered several attractions. I am not certain that some fibers of Mr. Garth's mind had not begun vibrating again toward the same end that was now becoming clear to Fred. An accident produces results only as a spark does where oil and tinder are ready; and Fred always felt that the railway had supplied the necessary spark. They continued in silence except when the work required them to speak. At last, when they had finished and were walking away, Mr. Garth said:
“A young man doesn't need a B.A. to do work like this, does he, Fred?”
“I wish I'd started it before ever thinking of getting a B.A.,” Fred answered. He hesitated, then added less confidently, “Do you think I'm too old to learn your business, Mr. Garth?”

“My business covers all sorts of things, my boy,” Mr. Garth said with a smile. “Much of what I know only comes with experience. You can't learn it by heart as you do things in a book. But you're still young enough to build a foundation.” Caleb spoke that last sentence firmly, then paused uncertainly. Lately he had understood that Fred had decided to enter the Church.
“You think I could be some use at it, then, if I tried?” Fred asked more eagerly.

“That depends,” Caleb said. He tilted his head and lowered his voice, with the air of someone saying something deeply religious. “You must be certain of two things. First, you must love your work, instead of always looking past it and wishing your free time would begin. Second, you mustn't be ashamed of the work, or think some other occupation would give you more standing. You must take pride in what you do and in learning to do it properly. No forever saying, There's this job and that job—if I had one of those, I could make something of it. Whatever a man does, I wouldn't give twopence for him”—Caleb's mouth tightened bitterly and he snapped his fingers—“whether he's prime minister or thatches haystacks, if he doesn't do well what he's undertaken.”
“I can never feel I'd do that as a clergyman,” Fred said, intending to advance his argument.
“Then don't become one, my boy,” Caleb answered abruptly. “Otherwise you'll never be comfortable with yourself. Or if you _are_ comfortable, you'll be a poor sort of man.”

“That's almost exactly Mary's view,” said Fred, blushing. “I think you must know how I feel about her, Mr. Garth. I hope it doesn't displease you that I've always loved her more than anyone else, and that I'll never love anyone the way I love her.”
As Fred spoke, Caleb's expression visibly softened. But he moved his head with solemn slowness and said:
“That makes it a more serious matter, Fred, if you want Mary's happiness entrusted to you.”

“I know it does, Mr. Garth,” Fred said eagerly, “and I'd do anything for _her_. She says she'll never marry me if I enter the Church. I'll be the most miserable devil alive if I lose all hope of Mary. Truly, if I could find another profession, some business—anything I'm remotely suited to—I'd work hard. I'd earn your respect. I'd like work that involved being outdoors. I already know quite a lot about land and cattle. I used to believe—you'll think it foolish, I know—that I'd have land of my own. I'm sure I could learn that sort of thing easily, especially if I could work under you in some way.”
“Steady, my boy,” said Caleb, seeing “Susan” in his mind's eye. “What have you told your father about this?”

“Nothing yet, but I must tell him. I'm only waiting to find out what I can do instead of going into the Church. I'm very sorry to disappoint him, but surely a man of twenty-four ought to be allowed to decide for himself. How could I have known at fifteen what would be right for me now? My education was a mistake.”
“But listen, Fred,” Caleb said. “Are you certain Mary loves you, or would ever marry you?”

“I asked Mr. Farebrother to speak to her, because she'd forbidden me to—I didn't know what else to do,” Fred said apologetically. “He says I have every reason to hope, if I can establish myself honorably—I mean, outside the Church. You probably think I've no right to trouble you and press my wishes about Mary on you, Mr. Garth, before I've done anything for myself. Of course I've no claim on you at all. In fact, I already owe you a debt that will never be paid off, even when I can repay the money.”

“Yes, my boy, you do have a claim,” Caleb said with deep feeling. “Young people can always claim help from older ones in making a start. I was young once and had to manage with very little help. I'd have welcomed it, if only for the kindness it showed. But I must think. Come to my office tomorrow at nine. The office, mind you.”

Mr. Garth never took an important step without consulting Susan. Nevertheless, it must be admitted that before he got home he had made up his mind. On a great many subjects about which other men were firm or stubborn, he was the easiest man imaginable to manage. He never knew which meat he preferred. If Susan had said they ought to move into a four-room cottage to save money, he would have answered, “Let's go,” without asking for details. But where Caleb's feelings and judgment spoke strongly, he ruled. Despite his gentleness and his reluctance to rebuke anyone, everyone around him knew that on the rare occasions when he chose to insist, he was absolute. Indeed, he only ever chose to insist on someone else's behalf. Mrs. Garth settled ninety-nine points; on the hundredth, she often discovered she must perform the exceptionally difficult task of practicing her own principle and accepting a subordinate place.

“It's turned out as I thought, Susan,” Caleb said when they sat alone that evening. He had described the incident that led Fred to help with his work, but had not yet told her what followed. “The children _are_ fond of each other—I mean Fred and Mary.”
Mrs. Garth lowered her sewing to her lap and fixed her sharp eyes anxiously on her husband.

“After we finished, Fred told me everything. He can't bear the idea of being a clergyman, and Mary says she won't marry him if he becomes one. The boy wants to work under me and turn his mind to business. I've decided to take him on and make a man of him.”
“Caleb!” Mrs. Garth said in a deep contralto that expressed astonishment and resignation together.

“It's a fine thing to do,” Mr. Garth said, settling firmly against the back of his chair and gripping its arms. “He'll give me trouble, but I think I can see it through. The boy loves Mary, and real love for a good woman is a great thing, Susan. It gives shape to many a rough fellow.”
“Has Mary said anything to you about it?” Mrs. Garth asked, secretly a little hurt that she herself had to be told.

“Not a word. I asked about Fred once and gave her a little warning. She assured me she'd never marry an idle, self-indulgent man. Nothing since. But apparently Fred got Mr. Farebrother to speak to her, since she'd forbidden him to speak for himself. Mr. Farebrother discovered that she is fond of Fred, but says he mustn't enter the Church. I can see that Fred's heart is set on Mary. It makes me think well of the boy—and we've always liked him, Susan.”
“I think it's a pity for Mary,” Mrs. Garth said.
“A pity? Why?”
“Because she could have had a man worth twenty Fred Vincys, Caleb.”
“Really?” said Caleb, surprised.

“I'm firmly convinced Mr. Farebrother loves her and intended to propose. Naturally, now that Fred has made him his messenger, that better prospect is finished.” Mrs. Garth spoke with severe precision. She was irritated and disappointed, but determined to waste no words.
Conflicting feelings kept Caleb silent for a few moments. He looked at the floor, moving his head and hands in accompaniment to an inward argument. Finally he spoke:

“That would have made me very proud and happy, Susan. I'd have been glad for your sake. I've always felt that the people belonging to you weren't your equals. Yet you chose me, though I was a plain man.”
“I chose the best and cleverest man I'd ever known,” said Mrs. Garth, quite certain that _she_ could never have loved anyone who fell below that standard.

“Well, perhaps others thought you could have done better. But it would have been worse for me. That's what touches me so closely about Fred. At heart he's good, and he's clever enough to do well if he's set on the right path. He loves and respects my daughter above everything, and she's given him a sort of promise, depending on how he turns out. That young man's soul is in my hands, I tell you. I'll do the best I can for him, so help me God! It's my duty, Susan.”

Mrs. Garth seldom cried, but before her husband finished speaking, a large tear was rolling down her cheek. It came from several feelings pressing together, much affection among them and some irritation. She quickly wiped it away and said:
“Not many men besides you would think it their duty to add to their worries like that, Caleb.”
“What other men think doesn't matter. I have a clear feeling inside me, and I'll follow it. I hope your heart will be with mine, Susan, in making everything as easy as possible for Mary, poor child.”
Leaning back, Caleb looked toward his wife with an anxious appeal. She stood and kissed him. “God bless you, Caleb! Our children have a good father.”

But she went out and cried thoroughly to make up for everything she had left unsaid. She was certain people would misunderstand her husband's actions. Her own judgment of Fred was rational and offered little hope. Which would prove more farsighted: her rationality or Caleb's passionate generosity?
When Fred arrived at the office next morning, he faced a test he had not anticipated.

“Now, Fred,” Caleb said, “there'll be desk work for you. I've always done plenty of writing myself, but I need help. I want you to understand the accounts and get the property values into your head, so I intend to manage without another clerk. You'll have to apply yourself. How are your handwriting and arithmetic?”

Fred's heart gave an uncomfortable jump. Desk work had never occurred to him. But he was feeling determined and would not back away. “Arithmetic doesn't worry me, Mr. Garth. I've always found it easy. I think you've seen my handwriting.”

“Let's have a look,” said Caleb. He picked up a pen, inspected it carefully, dipped it thoroughly, and handed it to Fred with a sheet of ruled paper. “Copy a line or two of that valuation, including the figures at the end.”

At that time people believed it beneath a gentleman to write legibly, or in any hand remotely fit for a clerk. Fred copied the lines in handwriting as gentlemanly as any contemporary viscount's or bishop's. All the vowels looked alike; the consonants could only be told apart by whether they pointed upward or downward. The strokes were solid with inkblots, and the letters scorned to follow the ruled lines. In short, it was the venerable sort of manuscript easily understood if you already know what its writer means.

As Caleb watched, his face grew increasingly downcast. When Fred handed him the sheet, he gave something like a growl and struck it angrily with the back of his hand. Work this bad drove away all Caleb's gentleness.

“Damn it!” he growled. “To think we live in a country where a man's education can cost hundreds upon hundreds of pounds and produce this!” Then, more sorrowfully, he pushed up his spectacles and looked at the unfortunate writer. “Lord have mercy, Fred, I can't accept this!”
“What can I do, Mr. Garth?” Fred asked. He was deeply discouraged, not only by the verdict on his handwriting but by the prospect of being classed with office clerks.

“Do? Learn to shape your letters and stay on the line. What use is writing if no one can read it?” Caleb asked forcefully, entirely absorbed by the poor workmanship. “Is there so little work to do in the world that you need to send puzzles all over the country? But that's how people are brought up. I'd waste endless time on some people's letters if Susan didn't decipher them for me. It's disgraceful.” He flung the paper aside.

A stranger looking into the office just then might have wondered what drama was unfolding between the indignant businessman and the handsome young fellow whose fair complexion was turning blotchy as he bit his lip in humiliation. Many thoughts struggled inside Fred. Mr. Garth had been so kind and encouraging when they first met that morning that gratitude and hope had risen high; now his spirits fell just as far. He had never considered desk work. In fact, like most young gentlemen, he wanted an occupation with nothing unpleasant about it. I cannot say what might have happened if he had not firmly promised himself that he would visit Mary at Lowick and tell her he had been engaged to work under her father. He did not want to lose that pleasure.
“I'm very sorry” was all he could manage to say. But Mr. Garth was already softening.

“We'll have to make the best of it, Fred,” he began in his usual quiet voice. “Anyone can learn to write. I taught myself. Set to it with determination, and stay up at night if you haven't enough time in the day. We'll be patient, my boy. Callum can keep doing the books while you're learning. But I must be off now,” Caleb said, getting up. “Tell your father what we've agreed. Once you can write, you'll save me Callum's salary, you see. I can afford to pay you eighty pounds for the first year, and more afterward.”

When Fred gave his parents the necessary news, the difference in their reactions surprised him and left a deep impression on his memory. He went directly from Mr. Garth's office to the warehouse. He rightly felt that he could show his father most respect by making this painful announcement as seriously and formally as possible. His decision would also be more clearly understood as final if he presented it during his father's most serious hours, which were always those spent in his private room at the warehouse.

Fred came straight to the point. He briefly explained what he had done and what he intended to do, ending by expressing his sorrow at disappointing his father and blaming his own shortcomings. That sorrow was real, and gave him strong, simple words.

Mr. Vincy listened in profound surprise without even an exclamation. In someone so impatient, this silence signaled unusual emotion. Business had already left him in low spirits that morning. As he listened, the slight bitterness around his mouth grew intense. After Fred finished, nearly a minute passed. Mr. Vincy put a book back in his desk and turned the key decisively. Then he looked steadily at his son and said:
“So you've finally decided, have you, sir?”
“I have, father.”
“Very well. Keep to your decision. I've nothing more to say. You've wasted your education and moved down in the world when I gave you the means to rise. That's all.”
“I'm very sorry we disagree, father. I believe I can be as much a gentleman in this work as I could have been as a curate. But I'm grateful that you wanted the best for me.”
“Very well. There's nothing more to say. I wash my hands of you. I only hope that when you have a son, he repays the trouble you take over him better than this.”

This hurt Fred deeply. His father was using the unfair advantage available to us all when we find ourselves in a pitiable position and view our past as though it too were simply part of what deserves sympathy. In truth, Mr. Vincy's ambitions for his son had contained considerable pride, thoughtlessness, and selfish folly. Nevertheless, the disappointed father possessed powerful leverage. Fred felt as if he were being sent away under a curse.
“I hope you won't object to my staying at home, sir?” he said, getting up to leave. “My salary will be enough to pay for my board, which of course I'd wish to do.”

“Board be damned!” said Mr. Vincy, recovering himself in disgust at the suggestion that feeding Fred would make a noticeable difference at his table. “Your mother will want you to stay, naturally. But I won't keep a horse for you, understand, and you'll pay your own tailor. I expect you'll manage with a suit or two less when you're buying them yourself.”
Fred stayed a moment. There was something else he needed to say. At last it came out.
“I hope you'll shake my hand, father, and forgive me for the distress I've caused you.”
Still seated, Mr. Vincy glanced quickly up at his son, who had moved closer. He held out his hand and said hurriedly, “Yes, yes. Let's say no more about it.”

With his mother Fred went through a much fuller account and explanation. But she could not be consoled. She saw something her husband perhaps had never considered: the certainty that Fred would marry Mary Garth. From then on, her own life would be spoiled by an endless influx of Garths and their habits. Her darling boy, with his beautiful face and stylish manner “beyond any other son in Middlemarch,” would surely grow like them in plainness and indifference to clothes. To her, the Garths seemed to have conspired to capture the desirable Fred. She dared not develop that view, however, because even a slight suggestion of it had made him “fly out” at her as never before. She was too sweet-tempered to show anger, but felt her happiness had been bruised. For several days, simply looking at Fred brought a few tears, as if some dreadful prophecy hung over him. Perhaps she recovered her usual cheerfulness more slowly because Fred had warned her not to reopen the painful subject with his father, who had accepted his choice and forgiven him. Had her husband attacked Fred vehemently, she would have been stirred to defend her darling. It was not until the end of the fourth day that Mr. Vincy said:
“Come now, Lucy, my dear, don't be so miserable. You've always spoiled the boy. You'll just have to keep on spoiling him.”
“Nothing's ever hurt me this much, Vincy,” his wife said, her fair throat and chin starting to tremble again, “except when he was ill.”
“Oh, come, never mind! We have to expect trouble with our children. Don't make it worse by letting me see you so unhappy.”
“Well, I won't,” said Mrs. Vincy. The appeal roused her, and she gave herself a small settling shake, like a bird smoothing its ruffled feathers.
“We can't start making such a fuss over one of them,” said Mr. Vincy, wanting to combine a little grumbling with domestic cheerfulness. “There's Rosamond as well as Fred.”
“Yes, poor thing. I was so sorry she lost her baby. But she's recovered nicely.”

“Baby, indeed! I can see Lydgate's making a mess of his practice, and from what I hear he's getting into debt as well. One of these days Rosamond will come to me with a fine story. But they'll get no money from me, I can tell you. Let _his_ family help. I never liked that marriage. Still, talking's no use. Ring for lemons, and stop looking miserable, Lucy. I'll drive you and Louisa to Riverston tomorrow.”

chapters.title: Book VI: The Widow And The Wife — Chapter LVII
paragraphs:
They were scarcely eight when a name
Stirred in their souls the secret movements
That make buds tremble and shape their hidden growth
As life-giving air enters them:
The name of him who told of faithful Evan Dhu,
Of odd Bradwardine, and Vich Ian Vor,
Enlarging childhood's little world
With mountains, lakes, and rocky heights,
And larger still with wonder, love, and faith
In Walter Scott, who from far away
Sent them this wealth of joy and noble sorrow.
They had to part with the book, but day by day,
In lines like plump spiders running sideways,
They copied out the story, from Tully Veolan.

On the evening Fred Vincy walked to Lowick Parsonage, he left at five and called on Mrs. Garth along the way. He wanted to make sure she willingly accepted the new connection between them. He was beginning to realize that even a spirited young man must sometimes walk through this world because he has no horse to carry him.

He found the family, cats and dogs included, beneath the orchard's great apple tree. For Mrs. Garth it was a festive occasion: her eldest son Christy, her special pride and joy, had come home for a short holiday. Christy thought nothing could be more desirable than becoming a tutor, studying every literature, and turning himself into a new Porson. To poor Fred, he was criticism in human form, an object lesson supplied by that educational mother. Christy himself was a broad-shouldered, square-browed male version of his mother, and barely reached Fred's shoulder—which made having to acknowledge his superiority still harder. He was completely unpretentious. Fred's lack of scholarly ambition interested him no more than a giraffe's would have; he only wished he shared more of Fred's height. Just now he lay on the ground beside his mother's chair with his straw hat flat over his eyes. On her other side, Jim was reading aloud from that beloved author responsible for so much happiness in many young lives. The book was “Ivanhoe,” and Jim had reached the great archery scene at the tournament. Ben kept interrupting him. He had fetched his old bow and arrows and, in Letty's opinion, was making himself horribly disagreeable by demanding that everyone watch his erratic shots. No one wanted to except Brownie, the lively-minded but probably shallow mongrel. The gray-haired Newfoundland lay in the sun and watched with the dull-eyed indifference of extreme old age. Letty's mouth and pinafore bore slight evidence of her help in gathering the cherries heaped like coral on the tea table. Now she sat wide-eyed on the grass, listening to the story.

Fred Vincy's arrival changed everyone's focus. Sitting down on a garden stool, he said he was heading to Lowick Parsonage. Ben dropped his bow, seized an unwilling half-grown kitten instead, stepped over Fred's outstretched leg, and said, “Take me with you!”
“Me too, please!” Letty said.
“You couldn't keep up with me and Fred,” said Ben.
“I could. Mother, please tell them I can go,” Letty pleaded. Much of her life consisted of resisting being thought less capable because she was a girl.
“I'm staying with Christy,” Jim remarked, implying that he had got the better of those simpletons. Letty put a hand to her head and looked jealously from one to another, unable to decide.
“Why don't we all go and see Mary?” Christy said, spreading his arms.

“No, my dear boy, we mustn't descend on the parsonage in a swarm. And that old Glasgow suit of yours won't do at all. Besides, your father will be coming home. We must leave Fred to go by himself. He can tell Mary you're here, and she'll come back tomorrow.”

Christy looked down at his threadbare knees, then at Fred's lovely white trousers. Fred's tailoring certainly made a case for the advantages of an English university. Even looking hot and pushing back his hair with a handkerchief, he managed to be graceful.
“Children, off you go,” said Mrs. Garth. “It's too warm to crowd round your friends. Take your brother to see the rabbits.”
Her eldest understood and immediately led the children away. Fred realized that Mrs. Garth wanted to let him say whatever he had come to say, but he could only begin with:
“You must be so pleased to have Christy home.”

“Yes, he's arrived earlier than I expected. He got off the coach at nine, just after his father left. I can't wait for Caleb to come back and hear how wonderfully Christy is progressing. For the past year he's covered his expenses by teaching while studying hard himself. He hopes to secure a private tutor's post soon and travel abroad.”

“He's a splendid fellow,” Fred said. These cheerful truths tasted like medicine to him. “And never a trouble to anyone.” After a short pause he added, “But I'm afraid you think I'll be a great deal of trouble to Mr. Garth.”

“Caleb enjoys taking trouble. He's one of those men who always do more than anyone would have thought to ask,” Mrs. Garth replied. She was knitting, which allowed her to look at Fred or not, just as she pleased—always useful when one wants to load a conversation with improving lessons. Though she meant to be properly restrained, she did want to say something that would do Fred good.

“I know you think I deserve very little, Mrs. Garth, and you're right,” said Fred, beginning to bristle as he detected a readiness to lecture him. “I've managed to behave worst toward the very people I can't help wanting most from. But while men like Mr. Garth and Mr. Farebrother haven't given up on me, I don't see why I should give up on myself.” He thought these male examples might usefully be brought to Mrs. Garth's attention.
“Certainly,” she said with increasing emphasis. “A young man for whom two such older men had devoted themselves would be seriously at fault if he wasted his life and made their sacrifices useless.”

Her forceful language puzzled Fred a little. He answered only, “I hope that won't happen to me, Mrs. Garth, now I've been given some reason to believe I may win Mary. Mr. Garth told you about that? I don't suppose it surprised you?” He meant innocently that his own love had probably been plain enough.

“Surprised that Mary had given you encouragement?” Mrs. Garth replied. She thought Fred ought to understand more clearly that, whatever the Vincys might imagine, Mary's friends could never have wished for this beforehand. “Yes, I admit I was surprised.”
“She never gave me any—not the slightest—when I spoke to her myself,” Fred said, eager to defend Mary. “But when I asked Mr. Farebrother to speak on my behalf, she let him tell me there was hope.”

The impulse to admonish Fred had begun stirring in Mrs. Garth and had not yet found full release. Even _her_ self-control struggled with the sight of this flourishing young man thriving on the disappointments of sadder, wiser people—eating a nightingale without knowing it—while his family imagined hers desperately needed this young sprig. Her irritation had fermented all the more vigorously because she had suppressed it completely with her husband. Exemplary wives sometimes find scapegoats this way. Now she said firmly and forcefully, “Asking Mr. Farebrother to speak for you was a great mistake, Fred.”

“Was it?” Fred instantly went red. He was alarmed but could not understand her meaning. Apologetically he added, “He's always been such a good friend to us. I knew Mary would listen seriously to him, and he agreed to do it very readily.”

“Yes, young people usually see nothing except their own wishes, and seldom imagine what those wishes cost others,” said Mrs. Garth. She intended to go no further than this beneficial general lesson. Instead, she released her indignation by unnecessarily unwinding her wool and frowning grandly at it.
“I can't imagine how it could have hurt Mr. Farebrother,” Fred said, though surprising possibilities were already beginning to take shape in his mind.
“Exactly. You can't imagine,” Mrs. Garth said, clipping each word as neatly as possible.
For a moment Fred stared toward the horizon in anxious dismay. Then he turned abruptly and asked, almost sharply:
“Are you saying Mr. Farebrother's in love with Mary, Mrs. Garth?”

“If he were, Fred, I should think you'd be the last person to find it surprising,” Mrs. Garth replied. She laid her knitting beside her and folded her arms. Putting her work down was an unusual sign of emotion. Her feelings were, in fact, divided: she was pleased to have taught Fred a lesson, but suspected she had gone too far. He picked up his hat and stick and stood quickly.
“So you think I'm in his way—and Mary's?” His tone seemed to require an answer.

Mrs. Garth could not reply immediately. She had put herself in the awkward position of being asked to state her real feelings when she knew there were strong reasons to conceal them. The knowledge that she had said too much was particularly humiliating to her. Fred had also displayed an unexpected spark. Now he added, “Mr. Garth seemed glad that Mary cared for me. He can't have known about this.”
The mention of her husband gave Mrs. Garth a sharp pang. She found the fear of Caleb's disapproval hard to bear. Hoping to prevent consequences she had never intended, she answered:
“I was only drawing an inference. I have no knowledge that Mary is aware of anything.”

Yet she hesitated to beg him to keep silent about a subject she herself had needlessly introduced. She was unused to humbling herself that way. While she hesitated, another rush of unintended consequences swept beneath the apple tree where the tea things stood. Ben bounded over the grass with Brownie behind him. Seeing the kitten trailing the knitting on a lengthening string of wool, he shouted and clapped. Brownie barked. The desperate kitten leaped onto the tea table, upset the milk, then jumped down and swept half the cherries with it. Ben snatched up the half-knitted sock top and pulled it over the kitten's head to drive it into a fresh frenzy. Letty arrived, protesting to her mother at the cruelty. It was a chain of events as sensational as “This is the house that Jack built.” Mrs. Garth had to intervene; the other young people joined them, and her private conversation with Fred ended. He escaped as soon as possible. All she could do to suggest some retreat from her severity was say “God bless you” while shaking his hand.

She was painfully aware that she had come close to speaking as “one of the foolish women speaketh”: telling something first, then begging for silence. But she had not begged for silence. To forestall Caleb's criticism, she decided to criticize herself and confess everything to him that night. It was curious how dreadful a tribunal gentle Caleb could establish for her whenever he chose. Still, she meant to point out that the revelation might do Fred Vincy considerable good.

It certainly affected him strongly as he walked toward Lowick. His light, hopeful nature had perhaps never been so bruised as by the suggestion that, without him in the way, Mary could have made an excellent marriage. He was also vexed at having been, as he called it, such a stupid fool as to ask Mr. Farebrother to intervene. But no lover could have kept this new worry about Mary's feelings from overtaking every other concern; Fred certainly could not. Despite his trust in Mr. Farebrother's generosity, and despite what Mary had said through him, Fred could not shake the feeling that he had a rival. This was a new awareness, and he disliked it intensely. He had no readiness at all to give Mary up for her own good. He was quite ready, instead, to fight any man for her. Fighting Mr. Farebrother, however, would have to be metaphorical, which was much harder for Fred than a contest of muscles. The experience disciplined him almost as sharply as the disappointment of his uncle's will. The iron had not entered his soul, but he had begun to imagine its cutting edge. It never occurred to him that Mrs. Garth might be mistaken about Mr. Farebrother. He did suspect she might be mistaken about Mary. Since Mary had lately been staying at the parsonage, her mother might know very little of what had been going through her mind.

Finding Mary cheerful in the drawing room with the three ladies did not reassure him. They had been talking animatedly about something they dropped as he entered. Mary was copying labels from a pile of shallow cabinet drawers in the tiny handwriting at which she excelled. Mr. Farebrother was somewhere in the village, and the three ladies knew nothing of Fred's special relationship with Mary. Neither of them could suggest a walk in the garden. Fred predicted that he would have to leave without a private word. He first told her Christy was home, then that he had arranged to work for her father. It comforted him to see how deeply the latter news moved her. “I'm so glad,” she said quickly, then bent over her writing to hide her face. But Mrs. Farebrother could not let such a subject pass.

“Surely, my dear Miss Garth, you don't mean you're glad a young man is abandoning the Church for which he was educated. You only mean that, since this is how matters stand, you're glad he'll be working under an excellent man like your father.”

“No, Mrs. Farebrother, I'm afraid I really am glad about both,” said Mary, skillfully disposing of one disobedient tear. “My mind is dreadfully secular. I've never liked a clergyman except the Vicar of Wakefield and Mr. Farebrother.”

“But why, my dear?” Mrs. Farebrother stopped her large wooden knitting needles and looked at Mary. “You always have good reasons for your opinions, but this amazes me. Naturally, I exclude those who preach new doctrines. But why should you dislike clergymen?”
“Oh dear,” Mary said, appearing to think for a moment before her face broke into amusement. “I don't like their neckcloths.”
“Then you don't like Camden's?” Miss Winifred asked anxiously.
“Yes, I do,” said Mary. “It's the other clergymen's neckcloths I dislike, because they're the ones wearing them.”
“How very confusing!” said Miss Noble, suspecting that her own intelligence was at fault.
“My dear, you're joking. You would need better reasons to dismiss such a respectable group of men,” Mrs. Farebrother declared majestically.
“Miss Garth has such strict ideas of what people ought to be that it's hard to satisfy her,” Fred said.
“Well, at least I'm pleased she makes an exception for my son,” the old lady replied.

Mary was wondering why Fred sounded so irritated when Mr. Farebrother entered and had to be told about Fred's arrangement with Mr. Garth. At the end he said with quiet satisfaction, “_That's_ right.” Then he bent over Mary's labels and praised her handwriting. Fred felt horribly jealous. Of course he was glad Mr. Farebrother was so admirable, but he wished the man were ugly and fat, as forty-year-old men sometimes are. The outcome was obvious: Mary openly ranked Farebrother above everyone, and these women were plainly encouraging the match. Fred was certain he would have no chance to speak to Mary when Mr. Farebrother said:
“Fred, help me take these drawers back to my study. You haven't seen my fine new study yet. Please come as well, Miss Garth. I want to show you a magnificent spider I found this morning.”

Mary immediately understood the Vicar's purpose. Since that memorable evening, he had never departed from his old pastoral kindness toward her, and her brief wonder and uncertainty had fallen completely asleep. Mary habitually judged probabilities with some rigor. If an idea flattered her vanity, she took that as a warning to reject it as absurd, a practice in which she had gained plenty of experience early in life. Things happened as she expected. After inviting Fred to admire the study's furnishings and Mary to admire the spider, Mr. Farebrother said:
“Stay here a moment. I'm going to find an engraving. Fred is tall enough to hang it for me. I'll be back in a few minutes.” He left. Yet the very first thing Fred said to Mary was:
“Whatever I do, it's useless, Mary. You're bound to marry Farebrother in the end.” There was anger in his voice.
“What do you mean, Fred?” Mary cried indignantly. She blushed deeply, startled out of her usual quickness in answering.
“You must see it perfectly clearly—you, who see everything.”
“All I see is how badly you're behaving, Fred, to speak like that about Mr. Farebrother when he's done everything to plead your case. How did you get such an idea?”
Despite his irritation, Fred showed some cunning. If Mary really had suspected nothing, there was no advantage in repeating what Mrs. Garth had said.
“It's the obvious conclusion,” he answered. “You're constantly with a man who's better than me at everything, and whom you put above everyone else. What fair chance can I have?”
“You're very ungrateful, Fred,” Mary said. “I wish I'd never told Mr. Farebrother that I cared for you at all.”

“I'm not ungrateful. Without this I'd be the happiest man alive. I told your father everything, and he was wonderfully kind. He treated me like his own son. I'd work with all my heart—writing and everything—if it weren't for this.”
“For this? What is ‘this’?” Mary asked, now imagining that something definite must have happened or been said.
“This awful certainty that Farebrother will bowl me out.” Mary's urge to laugh softened her anger.

“Fred,” she said, peering round to catch his eyes, which he had turned sulkily away, “you're delightfully absurd. If you weren't such a charming simpleton, I'd be terribly tempted to play the wicked flirt and let you think someone besides you had declared his love for me.”
“Do you truly like me best, Mary?” Fred turned his affectionate gaze toward her and tried to take her hand.

“At this moment I don't like you at all,” Mary said, stepping back and putting her hands behind her. “I only said no one alive except you has ever declared his love to me. That hardly proves any very wise man ever will,” she finished merrily.
“I wish you'd tell me you could never possibly think of him that way,” Fred said.

“Don't ever dare bring this up with me again, Fred,” Mary said, becoming serious. “I can't decide whether you're more foolish or ungenerous for failing to see that Mr. Farebrother deliberately left us alone so we could talk freely. I'm disappointed that you're so blind to his consideration.”

Before they could say more, Mr. Farebrother returned with the engraving. Fred went back to the drawing room still carrying jealous fears, but able to draw comfort from Mary's words and manner. On the whole, their conversation hurt Mary more. Inevitably, her attention had shifted, and she could see that things might be interpreted differently. She now felt as though she were slighting Mr. Farebrother. When the man concerned is greatly respected, that feeling always threatens a grateful woman's firmness. Having a reason to go home the next day was a relief, because Mary sincerely wanted never to doubt that she loved Fred best. When tender affection has accumulated within us over many years, the thought of exchanging it for anything else seems to diminish the worth of our lives. And we can guard our affections and our faithfulness just as we guard other treasures.

“Fred has lost every other expectation. He must keep this one,” Mary told herself, a smile curling her lips. She could not prevent passing visions of a different life: new dignity and the recognition of her worth whose absence she had often felt. But if Fred had no place in that life—if he were abandoned, looking sad because he had lost her—none of it could tempt her considered thoughts.

chapters.title: Book VI: The Widow And The Wife — Chapter LVIII
paragraphs:
“No hatred can ever live in your eyes,
So they cannot tell me when your feelings change.
In many faces a false heart's story
Appears in moods, frowns, and unfamiliar lines.
But when Heaven made you, it ordained
That sweet love should always dwell in your face.
Whatever thoughts you have, whatever stirs your heart,
Your looks should speak of nothing but sweetness.”
—SHAKESPEARE: _Sonnets_.

When Mr. Vincy voiced that foreboding about Rosamond, she had never imagined herself having to make the appeal he anticipated. She had not yet worried about money, though married life had been expensive as well as eventful. Her baby had arrived too early, and all the embroidered gowns and caps had to be put away in the dark. The loss was blamed entirely on her insistence on riding one day after her husband had asked her not to. But do not imagine that she had lost her temper or rudely declared she would do as she pleased.

Her particular desire to ride arose from a visit by Captain Lydgate, the baronet's third son. I am sorry to say that our Tertius Lydgate detested him as an empty-headed dandy who “parts his hair from forehead to neck in a contemptible fashion”—a fashion Tertius himself did not follow—and displayed an ignorant certainty that he knew the correct thing to say on every subject. Lydgate silently cursed his own foolishness: by agreeing to visit his uncle during their wedding tour, he had invited this visit upon himself. He made himself rather unpleasant to Rosamond by saying so in private. For her, the visit brought an unprecedented delight, gracefully concealed. She was so intensely aware that a cousin who was a baronet's son was staying in her house that she imagined everyone else's mind must be filled with the meaning of his presence. When she introduced Captain Lydgate to guests, she felt serenely certain that his rank reached them like a scent. For the moment, that pleasure dissolved some of her disappointment in the conditions of marriage to a medical man, even one of good family. Her marriage now seemed to lift her above Middlemarch visibly as well as in imagination. The future shone with letters and visits exchanged with Quallingham, and some vague resulting advancement for Tertius. Especially encouraging was the fact that, probably at the Captain's suggestion, his married sister Mrs. Mengan had stopped with her maid for two nights on her way from London. Clearly, then, it was worth Rosamond's while to practice her music and choose her lace with care.

Captain Lydgate's low forehead, aquiline nose bent to one side, and rather heavy speech might have counted against another young gentleman. He, however, had a military bearing and a mustache to supply what certain flower-like blond heads adored as “style.” He also possessed that kind of good breeding which consists in freedom from the little anxieties of middle-class gentility, and considered himself an expert judge of feminine attractions. Rosamond enjoyed his admiration even more here than she had at Quallingham. He found it easy to spend several hours each day flirting with her. Altogether, the visit was one of his most enjoyable adventures, perhaps all the more so because he suspected his odd cousin Tertius wanted him gone. Lydgate, who would sooner have died—figuratively speaking—than failed in courteous hospitality, concealed his dislike. He generally pretended not to hear the gallant officer's remarks and left Rosamond to answer. He was not at all a jealous husband, and preferred leaving an empty-headed young gentleman alone with his wife to keeping him company.

“I wish you'd speak more to the Captain at dinner, Tertius,” Rosamond said one evening when their important guest had gone to Loamford to see fellow officers stationed there. “You look so distracted sometimes. Instead of looking at him, you seem to be looking through his head at something behind it.”
“My dear Rosy, I hope you don't expect me to say much to such a conceited fool,” Lydgate answered brusquely. “If he cracked his head open, I might find it interesting to look at. Not before.”
“I can't understand why you speak so contemptuously about your cousin,” said Rosamond. Her fingers continued their work while she spoke with a gentle seriousness edged with disdain.
“Ask Ladislaw whether your Captain isn't the worst bore he's ever met. He's almost stopped coming here since the man arrived.”
Rosamond thought she understood perfectly why Mr. Ladislaw disliked the Captain: he was jealous. She liked his jealousy.

“There's no knowing what will please eccentric people,” she replied. “In my opinion, Captain Lydgate is a gentleman in every respect. Out of consideration for Sir Godwin, I don't think you should neglect him.”
“No, dear, but we've given dinners for him. He comes and goes as he pleases. He doesn't need me.”

“Even so, you could pay him more attention when he's in the room. Perhaps he isn't your idea of a miraculous genius. His profession is different. But it would do you good to talk about his interests a little. _I_ find him quite pleasant to talk to. And he's certainly a man of principle.”

“The truth is, Rosy, you'd like me to resemble him a little more,” Lydgate murmured with a sort of resignation. His smile was neither quite tender nor remotely cheerful. Rosamond said nothing and did not smile back, though the lovely contours of her face looked good-tempered enough without a smile.

Lydgate's words were a sad milestone, marking the distance he had traveled from his old dream world. There, Rosamond Vincy had appeared the perfect woman, who would revere her husband's intellect like some accomplished mermaid, using her comb and mirror and singing solely to relax the wisdom she adored. He had begun to see the difference between that imagined devotion and an attraction to a man's ability because it confers prestige, like a decoration in his buttonhole or “Honorable” before his name.

One might suppose Rosamond had also traveled some distance, since she had found Mr. Ned Plymdale's pointless talk unbearably dull. But most people find one kind of stupidity intolerable and another perfectly acceptable—otherwise, indeed, what would become of social ties? Captain Lydgate's stupidity wore a delicate fragrance, carried itself with “style,” spoke in a good accent, and was closely related to Sir Godwin. Rosamond found it very agreeable and adopted many of its expressions.

Rosamond, as we know, liked riding. She therefore had plenty of reasons to be tempted when Captain Lydgate encouraged her to ride his gray. He had sent for his servant and two horses to follow him and lodge at the “Green Dragon.” He guaranteed that the gray was gentle and trained for a lady; indeed, he had bought it for his sister and was taking it to Quallingham. Rosamond's first ride took place without her husband's knowledge, and she was home before he returned. But it had been such a success, and she declared herself so much better for it, that he was told with complete confidence that he would consent to further rides.

Instead, Lydgate was more than hurt. He was utterly bewildered that she had risked riding an unfamiliar horse without consulting his wishes. His first, almost thunderous exclamations of surprise gave Rosamond ample warning of what was coming. Then he fell silent for a few moments.

“Still, you've come home safely,” he finally said in a firm voice. “You won't go again, Rosy. That's understood. Even with the quietest horse you knew best in the world, an accident would always be possible. You know perfectly well that's why I wanted you to stop riding the roan.”
“An accident can happen indoors too, Tertius.”
“My darling, please don't talk nonsense,” Lydgate said imploringly. “Surely I'm the person best able to judge for you. My telling you not to go again ought to be enough.”

Rosamond was dressing her hair for dinner. In the mirror, the lovely image of her head changed only as she turned her long neck slightly aside. Lydgate had been moving around with his hands in his pockets. Now he stopped beside her, apparently waiting for reassurance.

“Will you pin up my braids, dear?” Rosamond asked. She dropped her arms with a little sigh calculated to shame a husband standing there like a brute. Lydgate had often pinned up her braids before. His large, beautifully shaped fingers made him exceptionally dexterous. He gathered the soft loops of plaited hair and secured the tall comb—such are the uses men come to! What could he do then but kiss the exquisite nape of her neck, with all its delicate curves exposed? Yet we often repeat an old action with a difference. Lydgate was still angry and had not forgotten his point.
“I'll tell the Captain he should have known better than to offer you his horse,” he said, moving away.
“Please do nothing of the kind, Tertius,” Rosamond said. She looked at him and spoke with more emphasis than usual. “That would be treating me like a child. Promise you'll leave the matter to me.”
Her objection did seem to contain some truth. Lydgate answered, “Very well,” with sullen compliance. So the discussion ended with a promise from him to Rosamond, instead of one from her to him.

In fact, she had determined not to promise. Rosamond possessed the triumphant stubbornness that never wastes energy on impulsive resistance. Whatever she wanted to do seemed right to her, and she directed all her intelligence toward finding a way to do it. She intended to ride the gray again. At the next opportunity, while her husband was away, she did so, meaning to keep him ignorant until his knowledge could no longer matter to her. The temptation was admittedly strong. She loved the exercise. The pleasure of riding a handsome horse with Captain Lydgate, Sir Godwin's son, beside her on another handsome horse—and being seen like this by anyone except her husband—was as good as her dreams before marriage. Besides, she was strengthening the connection with the family at Quallingham, which must be sensible.

But the gentle gray was unprepared for the crash of a tree being felled at the edge of Halsell wood. It startled, frightening Rosamond still more; this led eventually to the loss of her baby. Lydgate could not express his anger toward her, but he was rather gruff with the Captain, whose visit naturally ended soon afterward.

Whenever the subject arose later, Rosamond remained gently certain that the ride had made no difference. Had she stayed home, she said, the same symptoms would have appeared with the same result, because she had already felt something similar.

Lydgate could only say, “My poor, poor darling!” Yet privately he marveled at this gentle creature's terrible persistence. He was beginning to feel an astonished sense of his powerlessness over her. His greater knowledge and intellectual strength were not, as he had imagined, a shrine she would consult on every occasion. She simply disregarded them in every practical matter. He had considered her intelligence precisely the receptive sort appropriate to a woman. Now he was discovering its actual nature: the shape it had taken in a tight network of its own, separate and independent. No one saw causes and effects faster than Rosamond when they concerned her own tastes and interests. She had plainly recognized Lydgate's superiority in Middlemarch society, and could imagine still more delightful social advantages once his abilities had advanced him.
